blocks.text: Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) typically develops gradually. As iron stores are depleted, the body’s ability to produce hemoglobin the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen is compromised, leading to a variety of systemic symptoms.

runs.text: hemoglobin the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen is compromised, leading to a variety of systemic symptoms.

blocks.text: Anaemia according to WHO is a condition in which the number of red blood cells or their oxygen-carrying capacity is insufficient to meet physiologic needs, which vary by age, sex, altitude, smoking, and pregnancy status.

runs.text: insufficient to meet physiologic needs, which vary by age, sex, altitude, smoking, and pregnancy status.

These symptoms arise because the body’s tissues are not receiving enough oxygen (hypoxia):
Fatigue: The most common complaint; a persistent feeling of tiredness or lack of energy.
Dyspnea on Exertion: Shortness of breath during physical activity.
Palpitations: A sensation of a racing or irregular heartbeat as the heart pumps harder to compensate for low oxygen levels

runs.text: sensation of a racing or irregular heartbeat as the heart pumps harder to compensate for low oxygen

blocks.text: Pallor: Visible paleness, most easily observed in the conjunctiva (inner eyelids), mucous membranes, and nail beds.
Dizziness or Lightheadedness: Often felt when standing up quickly.
Certain physical signs are highly suggestive of iron deficiency specifically, rather than just general anemia:
Koilonychia: Also known as "spoon-shaped nails," where the nails become thin, brittle, and concave.
Glossitis and Stomatitis: A smooth, sore, or "beefy" red tongue and cracks at the corners of the mouth (angular cheilitis).
Pica: A specialized craving for non-nutritive substances. Common forms include: Pagophagia: Craving and chewing ice; Geophagia: Craving dirt or clay.

runs.text: ice; Geophagia: Craving dirt or clay.

blocks.text: Plummer-Vinson Syndrome: A rare triad of IDA, esophageal webs, and dysphagia (difficulty swallowing).
Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS): An irresistible urge to move the legs, often worsening at night.
Hemoglobin (Hb): The concentration of the oxygen-carrying protein. According to the WHO, anemia is generally defined as:
Hematocrit (Hct): The percentage of total blood volume made up of red blood cells (RBCs).
Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV): Measures the average size of RBCs. This is the most helpful value for classification:
Microcytic (Low MCV): Small cells; common in iron deficiency or thalassemia.
Normocytic (Normal MCV): Normal size; common in chronic disease or acute blood loss.
Macrocytic (High MCV): Large cells; common in B12 or Folate deficiency.
Dietary management (Refer FBDG & National Clinical Nutrition & Dietetics Guideline)
While diet alone is rarely sufficient to treat established anemia, it is crucial for maintaining levels once stores are restored.

Encourage consumption of foods rich in iron, folate, proteins and other nutrients needed for blood production. This includes: green leafy vegetables such as spinach, amaranths, pumpkin leaves, sweet potato leaves etc.; citrus fruits such as passion fruits, lemon, oranges etc.; beetroots & rosella etc.

Zinc deficiency is particularly prevalent among children under five and is a major contributor to stunting and recurrent infections.
Dietary management (Refer FBDG & Clinical Nutrition & Dietetics guideline)
Animal Proteins: Small fish (dagaa), poultry, and liver are the most "bioavailable" sources (easiest for the body to use).
Legumes: Beans and lentils (though these should be soaked or fermented to reduce phytates and improve zinc uptake).
Pumpkin Seeds: A locally available and highly potent plant source of zinc.
Food Fortification: fortification of wheat and maize flour with zinc (consider food fortification logo).
In Management of Diarrhea: Zinc is a mandatory part of the "Integrated Management of Childhood Illness" (IMCI) protocol.
